tutorial.text: Randy Popping. Forty years of muddy fields and missing headliners. Let's get you through your first festival without either.
You've got £{cash} to play with. Bands, toilets, food and the field all come out of that, so don't blow it on the headliner.
Three stars to chase: make a profit, keep the crowd happy, keep the bands happy. Get two and you're through to next year.
Three slots: opener, support and headliner. Start at the top. It's the headliner that sells the tickets.
This is {band_name}. Acts like this usually go for £{rate_low} to £{rate_high}. Make them an offer and see what comes back.
You've three things to play with: the fee, where they sit on the bill, and their cut of the merch.
A counter. That's a good sign: they want the gig. Meet them part way, or offer a bigger merch cut. Just remember their cut comes out of what you sell.
Signed. Remember what you paid. A happy band plays a better set.
Ah, they've walked. No harm done. Try another act.
Now the opener and support. Cheaper acts, and one of them might be the next big thing.
Now the field. Stage first, then toilets and food. 500 people need somewhere to go and something to eat, in that order.
This is your forecast. Change anything and it updates. It's a guess, not a promise, but it's a good guess.
A limiter's cheap insurance. Village folk complain about noise; they always have.
A fair price is £{fair_price}. Go above it and fewer come; go below it and the profit gets thin.
Gates are open. Keep an eye on the bars at the top: the crowd, the bands and your three targets.
There's a queue at the food stall. Get a food van in before tempers fray.
Good. Problems only get bigger the longer you leave them.
No queue at the food stalls. That's what planning buys you.
Your support act is stuck on the A-road. Stretch the opener's set, or fill the gap with music over the speakers.
Not a peep from the village. That limiter's earned its keep.
Someone's complained about the noise. Turn it down and the crowd grumbles; ignore it and you might get fined.
That's your headliner on. This is the bit everyone remembers.
Here's how you did: {stars} stars out of three.
Not bad at all. Next year they'll give you a bigger field and bigger names.
Not this time. Have another go, and I'll tell you what went wrong.
Want to skip the chat? Go on, I won't be offended.

festival2.text: The Local Field. Fifteen hundred people this time, so three times the toilets and three times the trouble.
Your cash won't stretch to a field this size, so the promoter's lending you £{advance}. It's paid back after the festival with a {fee}% fee, or {fee3}% if you earn all three stars.
Your reputation is {reputation} now. Some bands won't return your calls until it's higher. That's show business.
Four slots this time: an opener, two supports and a headliner.
You've got a bar. Beer's the best margin in the business, but a queue at the bar sours a crowd as fast as any other.
Rain's coming in. Ponchos or the covered area, your call. Do nothing and the crowd will tell you about it.
Two festivals in. People are starting to talk about you, mostly kindly.

festival3.text: Two Stages. Three thousand people and twice the bands. It gets complicated from here.
The second stage is for the smaller acts and the ones on their way up. Give an emerging band a slot here and watch them grow.
Watch your set times. Put two acts people love on at once and half the crowd goes home grumpy.
Two loud acts at the same time will drown each other out. Space them, or keep the quiet ones away from the loud ones.
The Last Heatwave won't play a festival with reputation under 75. You're at {reputation}. Something to aim for.
A band's pulled out. It happens. Book a replacement, but expect to pay over the odds at this short notice.
The toilets are out of order. Of course they are. Repair them or bring in a temporary block, and quickly.
Three festivals done. That's more than most manage. Next year, they'll want you to keep them overnight.

events.text: The bass amp's given up. Hire a replacement or let them play on without it. Bands remember who fixed things.
Your headliner's stormed off stage. Talk them round, or bring the support act back on. Just don't leave the stage empty.

tips.profit: You spent more than the day brought in. Next time, trim the lineup or nudge the ticket price.
tips.customers: The crowd went home grumbling. Look at your queues and your ticket price first.
tips.bands: The bands weren't happy. Pay closer to their asking price, and give them the slot they want.
